name: T-Bar Row

inherit.why: true for this child because the free-standing T-bar row is the same standing hip hinge with the back held straight while the arms pull (c2, c3).
true for this child because the Baechle and Earle rule covers all grips, the V-handle included (c19).
true for this child because it is also a heavy two-hand free-weight row; same MacDougall 1985 line (c16).
true for this child because it loads the lower back in the same bent-over position, more so without a chest pad (c11); same NHS back box (c18, c22).

claims.text: The free-standing T-bar row uses a barbell anchored in a landmine at one end, loaded with plates at the other, with a close-grip V-handle hooked under the bar about 8-10 inches from the plates.

quotes.text: Secure a barbell to a landmine attachment and load the free end of the bar with weight plates.
Hook a chinning triangle or close-grip dual handle about eight to 10 inches from the weight plate so it is facing upward.

claims.text: Stand over the bar, feet about shoulder width, knees slightly bent, and hinge forward at the hips.

quotes.text: Stand over the barbell with your feet about shoulder-width apart, bend your knees slightly, and hinge at the hips to lean forward.

claims.text: Hold the handle with both hands, brace, and keep the back straight with the chest parallel to the floor.

quotes.text: Grab the handle with both hands, engage your core, and keep your back straight so your chest is parallel to the floor.

claims.text: Pull toward the lower chest by pulling the shoulder blades back and driving the elbows back, then squeeze at the top.

quotes.text: Pull the barbell toward your lower chest by retracting your shoulder blades and driving your elbows back.
Contract your back muscles at the top of the movement.

claims.text: Lower slowly to the start, keeping tension in the back.

quotes.text: Slowly lower the barbell back to the starting position while maintaining tension throughout your back muscles.

claims.text: The hands on the handle are turned inward (palms facing each other).

quotes.text: Grasp the handle with both hands turned inward
quotes.where: How To Do T-Bar Rows At Home

claims.text: Rounding the back is one of the most common T-bar row mistakes; it strains the spinal erectors and raises the chance of a lower-back injury. Keep the trunk braced and use a load you can handle.

quotes.text: Lifters round their backs is one of the most common mistakes I see when training.
quotes.where: Common T-Bar Row Mistakes: Rounding Your Back

quotes.text: this loss of proper form can place a tremendous strain on your spinal erectors and ramp up your chances of suffering a lower-back injury. Keep your core engaged and use an appropriate load for your strength levels.
quotes.where: Common T-Bar Row Mistakes: Rounding Your Back

claims.text: Don’t swing from rep to rep; hold the squeeze at the top.

quotes.text: Avoid swinging from one rep to the next by holding the contraction at the top.
quotes.where: Common T-Bar Row Mistakes: Using Momentum

claims.text: Use the full range: don’t stop halfway down.

quotes.text: Don’t lower the weight halfway down, and do yourself a favor by executing the full repetitions to reap the most muscle-building rewards.
quotes.where: Common T-Bar Row Mistakes: Not Completing the Full Range of Motion

claims.text: The T-bar row mainly works the lats, rhomboids and erector spinae, with the biceps and rear delts supporting.

quotes.text: The T-bar row primarily engages the back muscles—the latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, and erector spinae. Meanwhile, your biceps and rear deltoids play supporting roles.
quotes.where: Muscles Worked by the T-Bar Row

claims.text: Without a chest pad, the lower back has to work much harder to hold the position.

quotes.text: However, when your chest isn’t supported, there are much higher demands on your lower back to maintain proper form.
quotes.where: How to Do the T-Bar Row

claims.text: On the chest-supported T-bar machine, set the foot plate so the sternum sits at the end of the pad.

quotes.text: Set the foot plate so that your sternum is at the end of the support bench.
quotes.where: Step 1 — Set Up and Take Your Grip

claims.text: Beginners start light and focus on form, adding weight gradually as strength and technique improve, in steps of about 2-10% once the target reps are beaten by one or two.

quotes.text: Beginners can safely perform the T-Bar row by starting with light weights and focusing on proper form. Gradually increasing the weight as strength and technique improve will help prevent injury and lead to progress.
When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: Tempo: about 1-2 s up and 1-2 s down, with a brief pause at the top and a slow lowering. ACSM gives its 1-2 s each way for intermediate to advanced lifters working toward heavy loads, so the seconds are a drawing convention; no source gives the top pause's seconds for a normal rep, so its 1 s is a drawing convention too (BarBend's pause line is written for the chest-supported T-bar, whose body angles it calls similar).

quotes.text: For intermediate (individuals with approximately 6 months of consistent RT experience) to advanced (individuals with years of RT experience) training
with eventual emphasis on heavy loading (1-6 RM) using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)
Avoid swinging from one rep to the next by holding the contraction at the top.
quotes.where: Common T-Bar Row Mistakes: Using Momentum

quotes.text: Slowly lower the barbell back to the starting position
After you lift the weights, pause slightly at the top to get a strong isometric contraction.

claims.text: Heavy lifting with a held breath (Valsalva) drives blood pressure very high.

quotes.text: It was concluded that when healthy young subjects perform weight-lifting exercises the mechanical compression of blood vessels combines with a potent pressor response and a Valsalva response to produce extreme elevations in blood pressure.

claims.text: In a lab comparison, the standing bent-over row gave the largest lumbar spine load of three rows; the free-standing T-bar row is also a standing bent-over row, so this likely applies (inferred, not measured on the T-bar).

quotes.text: The standing bent-over row produced large activation symmetrically across the back but produced the largest lumbar spine load.

claims.text: Back pain with weakness or numbness in both legs, or loss of feeling around the genitals, needs 999; pain not better after a few weeks needs a GP.

quotes.text: Call 999 or go to A&E if:
pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs
a loss of feeling around your genitals or anus
See a GP if:
it does not improve after treating it at home for a few weeks

claims.text: Wrap the thumbs around the handle.

quotes.text: Perform all grips with your thumbs around the bar.

claims.text: Lifting straps help on heavy rows when the grip limits the back work.

quotes.text: Lifting straps can aid your grip strength during heavy rows.
quotes.where: FAQs: Is it OK to use lifting straps with T-bar rows?

claims.text: Grip is strongest with the wrist in its natural extended (bent-back) position, about 35 degrees, and weakens when the wrist moves away from it, even to 15 degrees of extension (measured on a grip test, not on the T-bar row; applied here as a wrist cue).

quotes.text: The self-selected position was 35 degrees of extension and 7 degrees of ulnar deviation.
With the wrist in only 15 degrees of extension or in neutral radio-ulnar deviation, grip strength was reduced to two thirds to three fourths of normal.
Grip strength is significantly reduced when wrist position deviates from this self-selected optimum position.

claims.text: The NHS advises stopping back exercises if back pain gets worse and seeing a GP for advice (NHS advice on exercises for back pain, applied here to training).

quotes.text: But stop if your pain gets worse and see a GP for advice.
quotes.where: Exercises and stretches for back pain

claims.text: The row goes up as far as possible before the plates make contact with the torso; smaller plates on the bar, or the feet raised on plates or blocks, increase the range of motion.

quotes.text: Draw your elbows up and back, keeping them close to your body, rowing the weight up as far as possible before the plates make contact with your torso.
quotes.where: How to Do the T-Bar Row

quotes.text: Elevate your feet by standing on plates or blocks to increase the range of motion, alternatively you can use smaller plates on the bar for a similar effect.
quotes.where: How to Do the T-Bar Row

claims.text: Straddle the bar and hinge until the torso is near parallel to the ground; the handle passes under the barbell, behind the plates.

quotes.text: Straddle the bar and hinge at the hips until your torso is near parallel to the ground.
quotes.where: How to Do the T-Bar Row

quotes.text: Use a set of gymnastics rings, straps, a rope or even just a towel, passing it under the barbell, behind the plates to create a set of ‘handles’.
quotes.where: How to Do the T-Bar Row

plate.viewWhy: The chest-parallel back, the hinge and the handle path to the lower chest are front-to-back (c2, c3, c4); the census draws it side.
plate.equipment: Landmine rig: a barbell pinned at a floor pivot behind the lifter, plates on the free end, a V-handle hooked under the bar 8-10 inches from the plates (c1), behind the plates, with the lifter straddling the bar (c24). Smaller plates on the bar, or the feet raised on plates or blocks, give more range before the plates reach the torso (c23); the drawn plate size is a drawing convention (gaps). Needs the landmine composer (census gap).
plate.start: Standing over the bar, feet about shoulder width, knees slightly bent (c2), hips hinged, back straight, chest parallel to the floor (c3), arms straight down to the handle.
plate.end: Same back angle (c3); elbows driven back, handle pulled toward the lower chest, shoulder blades pulled back (c4); the row stops as far up as it goes before the plates make contact with the torso (c23).

checkpoints.label: Chest parallel
checkpoints.what: Back straight, chest level with the floor.

checkpoints.label: Soft knees
checkpoints.what: Knees slightly bent, hips hinged back.

checkpoints.label: Elbows back
checkpoints.what: Elbows drive back, handle to the lower chest.

mistake.what: Rounded back: the spine bends forward over the bar.
mistake.why: Named one of the most common T-bar mistakes, straining the spinal erectors and raising lower-back injury risk (c7) on an unsupported lift that already loads the lower back (c11, c17).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 1: the rounded back (c7). GGR says "Lifters round their backs is one of the most common mistakes I see when training." in its T-bar row mistakes list; it names how often this fault happens. If that line is read as about all training, which LR-31 sets aside, step 2 gives the same fault: it is the only named fault a quote ties to harm ("can place a tremendous strain on your spinal erectors and ramp up your chances of suffering a lower-back injury", c7). Set aside: GGR's "Be mindful of these common pitfalls to maximize the return on your efforts and minimize your chances of injury." is a list sentence; "It’s all too easy to use momentum" uses "easy to", not a frequency word, and states no harm; the range line states no harm. BarBend's "they risk performing rows with an excessively rounded back, unintentional cheating at form, and changing their back angles to be more upright" is a list of what regular gymgoers risk doing, with no harm named; its "One is usually wide while another is narrow." is about the grips and "often require you to remain bent over in a compromised position" is about heavy rows in general. Fenwick's "produced the largest lumbar spine load" (c17) is the exercise, not a fault. drawable stays true: the side view shows the rounded back, a still sign. Pick unchanged.

tells.text: Handle comes up toward your lower chest

tempo.text: Up 1 and down 2 keep ACSM's 1-2 s, stated for intermediate to advanced training (c15, WEAK; LR-15). BarBend's "pause slightly at the top to get a strong isometric contraction" (written for the chest-supported T-bar) asks for a brief pause right after the pull, and no source gives its seconds for a normal rep, so the 1 s pause is a drawing convention (c15; LR-33). GGR's "holding the contraction at the top" gives no seconds. The longer holds ("counting two to three seconds per rep", "holding the fully contracted position for a few seconds") belong to harder variations, not this rep.

plate.variantLine: Drawn: the free-standing (landmine) T-bar with a V-handle (c1). The library also allows a chest-supported T-bar machine: there the foot plate is set so the sternum is at the end of the pad (c12) and the lower back works less (c11). Claims c4, c5, c8-c10, c13, c15, c16, c19-c21 hold for both; c2, c3, c6, c7, c17, c22 and the back box are for the free-standing version (BarBend's machine offers wide, narrow and angled grips, so c6's turned-in hands hold only for the V-handle).

grip.type: Neutral: palms facing each other on a V-handle.
grip.handContact: Handle across the base of the fingers and top of the palm (pull archetype); straps allowed on heavy sets.
grip.wrist: Bent back into its natural grip position (about 35 degrees), not curled forward; grip weakens when the wrist moves away from it.

setup.step: Barbell in a landmine, plates on the free end.
Hook a V-handle under the bar about 8-10 inches from the plates.
Stand over the bar, feet about shoulder width, knees slightly bent.
Hinge, chest level with the floor. Grab the handle, palms facing.
Beat target by one or two reps? Add 2 to 10 percent.

posture.point: Brace. Back straight, chest parallel to the floor.
Shoulder blades pull back as the elbows drive back.
Hold the squeeze at the top. No swinging.

handlingMistakes.fix: Brace and use a lighter load.
Hold the squeeze at the top of each rep.
Lower all the way each rep.

rows.where: Middle and sides of the back
rows.means: The lats, rhomboids and lower-back muscles do most of the work.
Without a chest pad, it works hard to hold the position.

rows.where: Pain in your back while rowing
rows.fix: Stop the set. Don't train through the pain.

risks.risk: A rounded back strains the lower back and raises the chance of injury.
Without a chest pad the lower back works much harder.
Heavy reps with a held breath send blood pressure very high.

zooms.wrong: Thumbs alongside the handle, not wrapped.

zooms.right: Back straight, chest level with the floor, soft knees.

libraryDiff.why: Library primary mid_back and secondary lats, biceps, rear_delts fit (c10). The library lists no stabiliser; add lower_back as a stabiliser: the anchor names the erector spinae as a primary muscle (c10), and without a chest pad the lower back works much harder (c11).

notes: Drawing conventions (LR-4; LR-34 way 2; R-LB3-5): grip.handContact ("Handle across the base of the fingers and top of the palm (pull archetype); straps allowed on heavy sets.") and the drawn palm direction (palms facing each other, as grip.type states from c6) are drawing conventions, not claims. The drawn wrist, grip.wrist ("Bent back into its natural grip position (about 35 degrees), not curled forward; grip weakens when the wrist moves away from it."), is this card's convention until the hand lane decides the hold and pull wrists across cards (F-LB3-3). plate.start's "arms straight down to the handle" is a drawing convention too: no quote places the arms at the start.
gaps: Plate size (R-LB3-12 a): no read source gives a plate diameter or weight for this row. Men's Health says only that smaller plates on the bar, or the feet raised on plates or blocks, increase the range of motion (c23). The drawn plate size is a drawing convention.

Plates relative to the hands (R-LB3-12 b): the sources place the handle under the bar 8-10 inches from the plates (c1) and "behind the plates" (c24), with the lifter standing over or straddling the bar (c2, c24); none gives a distance from the plates to the feet or torso.
